title: Running with Scissors
full_review:
"Running With Scissors" (TriStar), adapted from author Augusten Burroughs' best-selling memoirs about his wildly unconventional adolescence in the 1970s, shows how his bipolar mother, Deirdre (Annette Bening), estranged from her ex-alcoholic husband, Norman (Alec Baldwin), gives up their son (Joseph Cross) for adoption.

A narcissist to the core, Deirdre -- with delusions of being a great poet whose oeuvre will be published imminently -- sends Augusten to be raised by her quack psychiatrist Dr.

Finch (Brian Cox) and his extremely eccentric family in a dilapidated house where a Christmas tree stays up for years, the family nibbles on dog food, and mountains of unwashed dishes clutter the kitchen. There's catatonic wife Agnes (Jill Clayburgh), daughters Hope (Gwyneth Paltrow), given to pointing to random pages in the Bible for guidance, and Natalie (Evan Rachel Wood), a nonconformist who longs to go to college and becomes Augusten's confidante, and 35-year-old Neil (Joseph Fiennes), a seriously unbalanced adopted son.

Director Ryan Murphy (who also wrote the screenplay) faithfully recreates the book's main episodes, though those unfamiliar with the original may find the narrative disconcertingly choppy and more than a bit puzzling. Still, he handles the provocative material with sensitivity, toning down the racier elements, the most troubling of which is 14-year-old Augusten's sexual relationship with Neil (mostly implied), and later, Deirdre's dalliance with a couple of women.

These, among other, situations are, in themselves, highly objectionable. However, the overall tone and ultimate resolution have a distinctly moral center, imparting clear messages about family, forgiveness and the need for boundaries in one's personal life. This last point is driven home with exquisite poignancy when, after living so long with no restrictions on his behavior whatsoever, Augusten cries out for moral structure.
The cast avoids caricature, though there is much mordant humor throughout at their expense. Bening has the showiest role and etches Deirdre's wild mood swings most skillfully, while Clayburgh is especially moving when she overcomes her lethargy and gives Augusten the maternal care she realizes he so desperately needs.

Amid an overall panorama of dysfunction and unconventionality, there are many surprisingly touching moments. Still, many Catholic viewers may find all the aforementioned problematic elements off-putting, if in fact they choose to spend time with the peculiar Finch brood at all.

The film contains pervasive rough language and profanity, a couple of discreetly handled same-sex relationships including a disturbing age-inappropriate one, other sexual themes and innuendo, scatological humor, drug use, domestic violence, an irreverent remark, and discussion of suicide. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
